title: Trump and Xi Toast Friendship at White House State Dinner, But No Deals Yet
summary:
President Donald Trump welcomed China's President Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday for a lavish state dinner, where both leaders emphasized a new chapter in their relationship. Trump toasted to "harmony, peace and success" and said, "We've never gotten along better." He presented Xi with a sculpture of a bald eagle, America's national symbol, adding that he and First Lady Melania had helped design it.

Xi thanked his hosts for their "meticulous care and consideration" and said the two countries "must act as responsible major countries to meet the expectations of our peoples." He described the relationship as "forged in blood and fire" during World War Two and later strengthened by Nixon-era "ping pong" diplomacy. Both leaders pledged to build a "constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability."

However, experts caution that the visit has yet to yield obvious progress on pressing issues like trade and technology. While the evening was heavy on flattery and cultural ties, the two sides remain divided on key disputes. The dinner also drew notable guests, including Elon Musk and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. As the leaders exchanged warm words, the real test will be whether their promises lead to concrete actions in the months ahead.
why_it_matters: The United States and China are the world's two largest economies and its two biggest military powers, so the tone between their leaders shapes everything from the price of phones to the risk of conflict. If a friendly dinner never turns into real agreements, the rivalry keeps hardening — and today's teenagers will live with the consequences.

background_read: A state dinner is a formal, carefully planned event at which a country's leader officially welcomes a visiting leader — with toasts, music and a fancy menu — and it is often used to show friendship even when the two governments disagree on big issues.

Donald Trump (the U.S. president, back in office since 2025) has favoured personal, face-to-face meetings with world leaders; Xi Jinping (China's president and head of its Communist Party since 2013) leads the world's second-largest economy.

The two countries have a long, complicated history. In 1972 President Richard Nixon became the first U.S. president to visit China, a breakthrough helped by 'ping pong diplomacy', when American and Chinese table-tennis teams played each other and helped ease decades of hostility.

Since then U.S. and Chinese leaders have met many times, but they still clash over trade, technology and Taiwan (a self-governing island that Beijing claims as part of China). That is why warm ceremonies rarely settle the hardest arguments.

perspectives.description: Supporters of the meeting argue that a friendly, high-profile dinner between Trump and Xi lowers tension and keeps the world's two biggest economies talking. They point to the shared language about a 'constructive' relationship of 'strategic stability' as a sign that both sides want to avoid a break.

Sceptics note the evening was 'heavy on flattery' while trade and technology disputes remain unresolved, and warn that photo opportunities can create a false sense of progress. In their view the real test — concrete action — has not yet been met.

Historians of U.S.-China relations point out that grand state visits have long been used to signal goodwill during tense periods, going back to Nixon's opening to China in 1972. Ceremony often buys negotiators time without settling the underlying disputes.

The question now is whether the pledges made over dinner turn into agreements on trade and technology, or fade once the cameras leave. If nothing changes, the next round of talks is likely to be far less friendly.
